title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
oneSentenceInsight: Better decisions begin when you recognize that your first intuitive answer may not be your best one.
summary: Daniel Kahneman explains two broad modes of thought: a fast, automatic mode and a slower, effortful mode. He uses research on heuristics, biases, judgment, and choice to show why people can make systematic errors even when they feel confident.
lessons: Human judgment is not automatically rational.
Fast intuition is useful, but it is vulnerable to predictable biases.
Important decisions deserve deliberate thinking.
Confidence is not the same as accuracy.
Structured processes can reduce recurring decision errors.
takeaways: Pause before high-stakes decisions.
Separate evidence from your first impression.
Use checklists for recurring important decisions.
Ask what evidence would change your mind.

chapters.title: The Two Systems
chapters.summary: Introduces fast intuitive thinking and slower deliberate reasoning.

chapters.title: Heuristics and Biases
chapters.summary: Shows how mental shortcuts can produce systematic judgment errors.

chapters.title: Overconfidence
chapters.summary: Explores why people can be confident while being poorly calibrated.

chapters.title: Choices
chapters.summary: Examines framing, risk, loss aversion, and decision behavior.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
oneSentenceInsight: Financial success is often less about intelligence than about behavior, patience, and staying in the game.
summary: Morgan Housel uses stories and observations to explain how behavior, luck, risk, time, and personal history shape financial decisions. The book emphasizes sustainable habits, long-term compounding, and defining what is enough.
lessons: Money decisions are deeply influenced by personal experience.
Compounding rewards patience.
Wealth is often the money you do not spend.
Room for error increases your chance of surviving uncertainty.
A financial strategy must fit your goals and temperament.
takeaways: Build a meaningful cash buffer.
Avoid strategies that can permanently knock you out of the game.
Define what enough means before chasing more.
Favor sustainable returns over impressive short-term results.

chapters.title: No One's Crazy
chapters.summary: People make financial decisions from different experiences and incentives.

chapters.title: Luck & Risk
chapters.summary: Outcomes contain both skill and randomness.

chapters.title: Compounding
chapters.summary: Small advantages can become enormous when given enough time.

chapters.title: Freedom
chapters.summary: Money can provide control over how you use your time.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
oneSentenceInsight: Lasting improvement comes from designing systems that make the right behavior easier to repeat.
summary: James Clear presents a practical framework for building good habits and breaking bad ones. The approach focuses on identity, environment, cues, rewards, and small improvements that compound over time.
lessons: Tiny improvements can compound.
Identity-based habits are more durable than goal-only thinking.
Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying.
Environment can be stronger than willpower.
Consistency matters more than occasional intensity.
takeaways: Make the desired behavior visible.
Start with a version of the habit that takes two minutes or less.
Pair new habits with existing routines.
Review your systems weekly.

chapters.title: The Fundamentals
chapters.summary: Explains why small changes can produce remarkable long-term effects.

chapters.title: The 1st Law
chapters.summary: Make the desired behavior obvious.

chapters.title: The 2nd Law
chapters.summary: Make the desired behavior attractive.

chapters.title: The 3rd Law
chapters.summary: Reduce friction and make the behavior easy.

chapters.title: The 4th Law
chapters.summary: Make progress satisfying enough to repeat.

title: The Intelligent Investor
author: Benjamin Graham
oneSentenceInsight: The investor's edge is not predicting the market; it is demanding a margin of safety and controlling behavior.
summary: Benjamin Graham's classic presents a disciplined approach to investing based on valuation, diversification, margin of safety, and emotional control. It distinguishes investment from speculation and treats market volatility as something to manage rather than fear.
lessons: Price and value are not the same.
A margin of safety protects against errors and uncertainty.
Market quotations should serve the investor, not control them.
Temperament is a major investing advantage.
Discipline matters more than forecasting.
takeaways: Write your investment thesis before buying.
Define downside risk before focusing on upside.
Use valuation ranges rather than false precision.
Do not let market mood dictate your process.

chapters.title: Investment vs Speculation
chapters.summary: Defines the characteristics of an investment and separates them from speculation.

chapters.title: Mr. Market
chapters.summary: Uses a fictional market partner to explain emotional price movements.

chapters.title: Margin of Safety
chapters.summary: Argues for a buffer between price and estimated value.

chapters.title: Investor Temperament
chapters.summary: Shows why emotional discipline is central to long-term results.

title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
author: Eric Jorgenson
oneSentenceInsight: Build specific knowledge, use leverage responsibly, and design a life where wealth and freedom reinforce each other.
summary: A curated collection of Naval Ravikant's ideas about wealth creation, judgment, leverage, specific knowledge, happiness, and long-term thinking. It emphasizes building rather than merely trading time for money.
lessons: Specific knowledge can be difficult to automate or commoditize.
Leverage can multiply the output of good decisions.
Long-term relationships and reputation compound.
Wealth and status are different objectives.
Freedom requires both financial and psychological independence.
takeaways: Develop skills that feel natural to you but are rare in the market.
Look for scalable outputs rather than only hourly work.
Protect your reputation.
Optimize for long-term freedom, not short-term status.

chapters.title: Building Wealth
chapters.summary: Frameworks for creating wealth through ownership, leverage, and specific knowledge.

chapters.title: Learning
chapters.summary: Ideas about reading, judgment, and developing unique skills.

chapters.title: Happiness
chapters.summary: Perspectives on desire, peace of mind, and subjective well-being.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
oneSentenceInsight: The biggest opportunities often come from creating something genuinely new rather than copying what already works.
summary: Peter Thiel argues that startups should seek technological and strategic breakthroughs rather than incremental competition. The book explores monopoly, secrets, distribution, founders, and the importance of a contrarian but defensible vision.
lessons: Creating something new can be more valuable than copying.
Distribution is as important as product quality.
Strong businesses seek durable advantages.
Contrarian truths can reveal overlooked opportunities.
A focused market can be a better starting point than a huge generic one.
takeaways: Identify an overlooked problem.
Ask what valuable truth few people believe.
Design a defensible advantage.
Solve distribution before assuming a great product will spread.

chapters.title: The Challenge of the Future
chapters.summary: Contrasts incremental progress with creating genuinely new value.

chapters.title: Monopoly
chapters.summary: Explains why durable businesses seek differentiation and market power.

chapters.title: Secrets
chapters.summary: Encourages searching for important truths that remain underexplored.

chapters.title: Foundations
chapters.summary: Examines teams, founders, and the importance of early strategic choices.

title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
author: Charles T. Munger
oneSentenceInsight: Good judgment improves when you build a latticework of mental models and actively avoid predictable mistakes.
summary: A collection of speeches, lessons, and ideas associated with Charlie Munger. It emphasizes multidisciplinary thinking, incentives, inversion, patience, temperament, and avoiding stupidity as much as pursuing brilliance.
lessons: Use multiple disciplines to understand complex problems.
Incentives can strongly shape behavior.
Inversion is a powerful problem-solving tool.
Avoiding major mistakes is often more important than seeking clever wins.
Patience and temperament compound.
takeaways: Ask how a plan could fail before asking how it could succeed.
Study incentives whenever people behave unexpectedly.
Build knowledge across disciplines.
Stay inside your circle of competence until you have evidence to expand it.

chapters.title: Mental Models
chapters.summary: Introduces a multidisciplinary framework for better thinking.

chapters.title: Human Misjudgment
chapters.summary: Explores recurring psychological tendencies and errors.

chapters.title: Inversion
chapters.summary: Shows how thinking backward can expose risks and solutions.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
oneSentenceInsight: The ability to concentrate without distraction is a competitive advantage in an increasingly noisy world.
summary: Cal Newport argues that sustained, distraction-free concentration produces valuable cognitive work. The book presents rules for cultivating deep work, reducing shallow obligations, and building rituals around focused effort.
lessons: Deep concentration is a trainable skill.
Distraction fragments attention and raises switching costs.
Rituals make focused work easier to start.
Shallow work can expand unless deliberately constrained.
Downtime supports high-quality thinking.
takeaways: Schedule protected focus blocks.
Remove notifications during demanding work.
Define a clear outcome for each deep-work session.
Batch shallow communication.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Valuable
chapters.summary: Explains why focused work is increasingly economically valuable.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Rare
chapters.summary: Shows how modern workplaces can reward distraction and responsiveness.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Meaningful
chapters.summary: Connects craftsmanship and concentration with satisfaction.

chapters.title: Rules
chapters.summary: Provides practical strategies for cultivating focused work.

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey
oneSentenceInsight: Effectiveness grows from principles, proactive choices, priorities, and relationships rather than productivity tricks alone.
summary: Stephen Covey presents seven habits built around personal responsibility, priorities, mutual benefit, empathetic communication, cooperation, and continuous renewal. The framework moves from private effectiveness to interpersonal effectiveness.
lessons: You can choose your response to circumstances.
Begin with a clear picture of the person and life you want to build.
Prioritize important work rather than merely urgent work.
Seek mutual benefit in relationships.
Listen to understand before trying to be understood.
takeaways: Write a personal mission statement.
Plan around important priorities.
Have difficult conversations after understanding the other person's perspective.
Reserve time for learning and renewal.

chapters.title: Private Victory
chapters.summary: Builds personal responsibility, vision, and priority management.

chapters.title: Public Victory
chapters.summary: Applies the habits to trust, relationships, and cooperation.

chapters.title: Renewal
chapters.summary: Emphasizes continuous improvement across physical, mental, social, and personal dimensions.

title: Outlive
author: Peter Attia
oneSentenceInsight: A long life is not the only goal; the aim is to preserve meaningful function for as long as possible.
summary: Peter Attia discusses a preventive approach to longevity, emphasizing the major drivers of chronic disease, exercise, nutrition, sleep, emotional health, and individualized risk assessment. It frames healthspan as a central objective rather than focusing only on lifespan.
lessons: Healthspan and lifespan are related but not identical goals.
Prevention benefits from acting before disease becomes obvious.
Exercise is a major pillar of long-term function.
Risk assessment should be individualized and evidence-based.
Long-term health requires sustainable habits rather than quick fixes.
takeaways: Build sustainable exercise habits.
Track meaningful health indicators with qualified professionals.
Prioritize sleep and recovery.
Think in decades rather than short-term transformations.

chapters.title: The Four Horsemen
chapters.summary: Introduces major chronic disease categories that shape longevity.

chapters.title: Exercise
chapters.summary: Explores aerobic capacity, strength, stability, and movement.

chapters.title: Nutrition
chapters.summary: Discusses nutrition as an individualized tool rather than a single universal diet.

chapters.title: Sleep and Emotional Health
chapters.summary: Highlights recovery and psychological health as parts of long-term well-being.
